docs.text: Red Cedar Red Cedar is a quantum machine learning framework from Cascade Quantum. You train models on quantum simulators and quantum computers without having to master the low-level details of quantum technology. You bring a table of data; Red Cedar builds, trains and runs the quantum circuits. The redcedar Python package (the SDK) is how you use Red Cedar from notebooks, scripts and the command line. It talks to a Red Cedar server, which runs the circuits, so nothing quantum needs to be installed on your machine. Documentation Overview Documentation is organized into the following sections, each addressing a specific need. Quick Start The Quick Start is for first-time users. It walks you through installing the SDK, training a model on your own data and getting predictions from it, in a few lines of Python. A perfect way to get up and running quickly. Go to the Quick Start guide. User Guide The User Guide is the definitive reference for everything the SDK can do: connecting to a server, preparing data, training and evaluating models, predictions, explainable AI, dataset analysis, settings, running on quantum hardware, and the command line. Go to the User Guide . Examples Ready-to-use Jupyter notebooks and Python scripts show complete workflows, from a first model to dataset analysis and training in depth. Go to the Examples . Release Notes Red Cedar is continually evolving, with issues fixed and enhancements made to add features. This section presents a record of changes made to each released version. Go to the Release Notes . Known Issues As with most complex and evolving software, Red Cedar has several issues you may want to be aware of. It helps to know what to expect when working with different backends and settings. Go to the Known Issues . docs.text: About Red Cedar Red Cedar is a quantum machine learning framework developed by Cascade Quantum. It lets you train models on quantum simulators and quantum computers without having to master the low-level details of quantum technology. Models are defined as hierarchical operators rather than circuits, which allows them to be synthesized efficiently for any hardware backend. Training uses three techniques developed for Red Cedar: Sub-net initialization , which lets model training scale without running into barren plateaus. Bit-bit encoding , which encodes classical data efficiently. Exact coordinate update , which trains the parameters without a classical optimizer. Packages Package What it is redcedar The Python SDK: connect to a Red Cedar server, train, evaluate, predict, explain. Depends only on requests . redcedar-examples Example notebooks and scripts that use the SDK. Red Cedar server Prepares the data, builds and runs the circuits, and trains the models. The SDK talks to it over HTTPS. Circuits run on Qiskit simulators, on CUDA-Q (including multi-GPU execution), and on IonQ and IQM simulators and quantum computers. Related Repositories redcedar : the SDK source. redcedar-examples : the example notebooks. License The redcedar SDK is open source. See the LICENSE file in the repository for details. Version Current SDK version: 0.93.0 . Current server version: 0.93 (November 2026). See Release Notes for version history. © 2026 Cascade Quantum. All Rights Reserved.

docs.text: Examples The redcedar-examples repository has Jupyter notebooks and a script that use the SDK. Each one runs against a Red Cedar server: set REDCEDAR_URL and REDCEDAR_API_KEY before starting Jupyter (see Connecting to a Server ). git clone https://github.com/coherent-computing/redcedar-examples.git cd redcedar-examples pip install "redcedar[plotting]" jupyter notebook 01_quick_start.ipynb Notebooks Start with 01_quick_start.ipynb ; the others go deeper into one topic each and can be read in any order. Each notebook is saved with the output of a run, so you can read the results and plots on GitHub without running it. Notebook Shows 01_quick_start.ipynb The basic workflow, as in the Quick Start : train a quantum model on a CSV file of classified samples, classify the samples in a second file using the trained model, check the predicted classes, and see which features the model relies on (explainable AI) 02_dataset_analysis.ipynb How to understand a dataset before training: PCA, mutual information and quantum resource estimation, comparing two datasets, and analyzing your own CSV file 03_training_settings.ipynb How training settings change a model, one section per setting: seed (repeatable runs) and op_direction (order of the operators), and the settings saved with each model 04_training_in_depth.ipynb A closer look at training: loss and accuracy during training, layers and layer chaining, test accuracy over the course of training, results per class and per layer, choosing the train and test data, reusing trained models, and checking on or stopping a running job 05_regression.ipynb The Quick Start's steps for regression, where the model predicts a number: train, measure the model on its test rows (mean absolute error), predict values for samples in a second file, and check the predicted values. Regression does not work well yet in this release: the predictions are currently further off than guessing the average Scripts quick_start.py has the same steps as 01_quick_start.ipynb , as a plain Python script for running from the command line or a scheduler. Run it from the redcedar-examples folder ( python quick_start.py ); it saves its plots as PNG files there. More scripts will follow, and the same steps can also be run with the redcedar command . © 2026 Cascade Quantum. All Rights Reserved.

docs.text: PAL — Problems, Anomalies, and Limitations As with most complex and evolving software, Red Cedar has several issues you may want to be aware of. This section describes known P roblems, A nomalies, and L imitations. Being aware of these in advance can help avoid frustration. Limitations These are fundamental limitations in the current implementation. Some may be relaxed in future versions. Tasks and Data Explainable AI supports classification models only. Regression models ( task="regression" ) train, evaluate and predict, but explainable.run() refuses them. Predictions need the model's training data on the server. New rows are prepared the way the training data was (scaling, compression, encoding), and that preparation is rebuilt from the training data. If the training file is gone from the server, predictions and evaluation for that model fail. Regression predictions stay within the range of the training targets. The model encodes the target on num_qubits_target qubits (default 2, so 4 levels) as a fraction of the range between the smallest and largest training target. A prediction is the average of that fraction over the measured outcomes, so it can't fall outside that range, and its resolution depends on the number of target qubits. Only CSV files can be uploaded. You can train on the catalog datasets and on CSV files you upload, but you can't yet plug in your own data loaders. Server The server runs one job at a time. Jobs submitted while another job is running are queued and start in order. Only training can be stopped. Inference, explainable AI and the training replay run to completion once they start. Saved models are deleted after 24 hours. Each time the server starts, it deletes trained models older than 24 hours, and all but the 30 most recent. A model you trained yesterday may be gone after a restart. Size-based cleanup is planned to replace this. Workaround : to keep a model, copy its folder from server/training_results/ . A restart drops jobs that were running. When the server starts, it removes jobs that were running when it stopped. They are not restarted; submit them again. Queued jobs are kept. Run one server per Red Cedar folder. All servers started from the same red-cedar folder share its job database ( server/jobs.db ). This includes a Qiskit server on the host and a CUDA-Q server in a container that mounts the same folder. Two servers running at once take each other's queued jobs and can fail with disk I/O error . Stop one server before starting another. CUDA-Q CUDA-Q samples; the Qiskit simulator is exact. CUDA-Q always estimates probabilities from shots. When no shot count is set, training, validation and inference on CUDA-Q use 100 shots, while the Qiskit statevector simulator computes exact probabilities. Results on the two APIs therefore differ somewhat for the same settings and seed. Explainable AI on CUDA-Q uses 10000 shots; this is a temporary value and will become a setting. Seeds don't make MPI multi-GPU runs repeatable yet. In the circuit-parallel ( RC_PARALLEL=1 ) and hybrid ( RC_GPUS_PER_CIRCUIT ) modes, the execution library sets the CUDA-Q target again inside its multi-GPU code, which drops the seed. Results are valid, but two runs with the same seed can differ. Single-GPU runs, and runs that spread one circuit across several GPUs, are seeded normally. Qiskit On Qiskit, a seed fixes only the starting parameters when shots are used. With a shot count set, or on a hardware or fake hardware backend, the sampling itself is not seeded, so results vary from run to run. Default runs on the statevector simulator are exact and repeat. Anomalies These are not bugs per se, but behaviors worth knowing about. Seeds The same seed gives different results on Qiskit and CUDA-Q. Both start from the same parameters, but CUDA-Q estimates probabilities from shots and the Qiskit simulator computes them exactly (see Limitations), so training takes a different path. An unseeded run right after a seeded run can repeat. On a running server, the random state carries over from one job to the next. Two unseeded runs that each follow the same seeded run start from the same state and give the same result. To get different random starts, give each run its own seed. Data With test_size=0 the training log still prints test results. The training workflows test the model before and after training; with no test set, they test on a few training rows. Those results appear in the log but are not reported: the layer results have no test values. Regression targets that are whole numbers are treated as classes unless you say otherwise. The task type is detected from the target column, and a column holding only whole numbers (including values like 12.0 ) looks like class labels. Workaround : pass task="regression" to training.run() (or --task regression on the command line). Known Problems These are specific bugs or issues that may be fixed in future releases. Regression Regression predictions are not useful yet. On the Energy Efficiency example ( 05_regression.ipynb in the examples), the model predicts about the same value for every sample, near the top of the target range, and its mean absolute error is larger than that of always predicting the average training value. The training loss falls while the test loss does not improve. Classification is not affected. Output Training logs a DEBUG: line on every parameter update. The line comes from quantum_learning/optimizer.py and makes the server's training log much longer. The SDK shows it only with verbose="log" . It does not affect results. Tests tests/test_circuit_builders.py fails to import. It imports cudaq_builders.ansatz , which no longer exists (the module is now quantum_ansatz.py ). © 2026 Cascade Quantum. All Rights Reserved.

docs.text: Quick Start This guide walks you through installing the Red Cedar SDK, training a quantum machine learning model on your own data, and using it to make predictions. It takes two calls. Prerequisites Python 3.9 or later A Red Cedar server to run the circuits: either one running on your own machine, or a hosted server with an API key (see Connect ) Nothing quantum is installed on your machine by the SDK. The server builds and runs the circuits. Install pip install redcedar The only dependency is requests . Add [plotting] ( pip install "redcedar[plotting]" ) if you want matplotlib for the plots in the examples. Connect A server on your own machine. If you have the Red Cedar engine installed, start its server from the red-cedar folder: ./run_server.sh # Linux / Mac run_server.bat # Windows It listens on port 8002, and the SDK looks for it at http://127.0.0.1:8002 by default. The server only accepts requests with the key that run_server.sh sets (the line export BACKEND_API_KEY=... ), so give the SDK the same key, or set it once in your shell as REDCEDAR_API_KEY : import redcedar client = redcedar.connect(api_key="<the BACKEND_API_KEY value from run_server.sh>") print(client.status()) # {'ok': True, 'server_version': '0.93', 'sdk_version': '0.93.0'} Without the key, status() and the dataset list still work, but training, analysis and the other calls are refused. A hosted server. Pass its URL and your API key, or set them once in your shell as REDCEDAR_URL and REDCEDAR_API_KEY : client = redcedar.connect(url="https://<hosted-server-url>", api_key="your-api-key") A hosted server only accepts requests with a valid API key. Contact your Cascade Quantum representative to get one, or to get access to the Red Cedar user interface. If you already have access to the user interface, you can create your own key there, under API Keys . Your Data A CSV file with one row per example. The input features come first; the last column is the answer you want the model to learn: a class label (or a number, for regression). A header row is optional, but recommended: with one, Red Cedar knows your columns by name. radius,texture,perimeter,area,smoothness,diagnosis 17.99,10.38,122.8,1001.0,0.1184,M 13.54,14.36,87.46,566.3,0.09779,B ... Step 1: Train a Model model = client.training.run("my_data.csv", verbose=True) print(model["train_id"]) training.run() uploads the file, trains a model on the server, and waits until it's done. With verbose=True it shows the progress, and the test accuracy after each layer of the model. By default, 80% of your rows train the model and the other 20% are held back to test it, so the accuracy you see is measured on rows the model has never seen. Once you're happy with the result, you can train on all of your rows with test_size=0 . The train_id names your trained model. You use it for everything that follows. Every part of the model and its training can be set: the number of qubits and layers, the circuit structure, how the data is prepared, the number of iterations, the seed, the backend. Pass them as settings= , a dict or a .json / .toml file: model = client.training.run("my_data.csv", settings={"num_qubits": 6, "max_layers": 3, "seed": 123}) The Settings section of the User Guide lists every setting and how to set it. Step 2: Classify Samples Using the Trained Model Now use the trained model on samples whose class is not yet known. This file has the same input columns as the training file, without the class column, since the class is what you want to find out: results = client.inference.run(model["train_id"], "unclassified.csv") for row in results["predictions"][:5]: print(row["prediction"], row["probabilities"]) inference.run() returns one result per row: the predicted class, and the probability the model gives each class (the probability of the predicted class is the model's confidence). Using a trained model on samples it hasn't seen is called inference , hence the function's name. To save the results next to your data, add output="predicted.csv" . If the file does have the class column, the result also includes the accuracy. That's all it takes: a file, a trained model, and the predicted classes. One Step Further: Which Features Matter? Red Cedar can show which of your input features the model relies on to make its decisions: explanation = client.explainable.run(model["train_id"], verbose=True) for q in explanation["qubit_map"]: print(f"{q['feature_name']}: {q['importance']:.1%}") Each data qubit of the model encodes one input feature, and importance measures how much that qubit influences the prediction. By default Red Cedar first combines your columns into new features (principal components); train with settings={"dimension_reduction": "none"} to keep your own columns, so that the results name them. See Explainable AI in the User Guide. What Next There is much more you can control. The User Guide covers it all; some places to start: Regression : predict a number instead of a class, with task="regression" . Settings : every training option (qubits, layers, the circuit structure, data preparation, training, execution) and how to set it. Evaluate a model : the accuracy per class, for any layer, or on a different backend. Analyze a dataset before training: how many dimensions carry signal, and how many qubits the model needs. Run on quantum hardware : train on a simulator, run on a quantum computer. The command line : redcedar train my_data.csv , without writing any Python. The Examples have notebooks for analyzing a dataset, the training settings, and training and evaluating a model in depth. © 2026 Cascade Quantum. All Rights Reserved.

This file has the same input columns as the training file, without the class column, since the class is what you want to find out: results = client.inference.run(model["train_id"], "unclassified.csv") for row in results["predictions"][:5]: print(row["prediction"], row["probabilities"]) inference.run() returns one result per row: the predicted class, and the probability the model gives each class (the probability of the predicted class is the model's confidence). Using a trained model on samples it hasn't seen is called inference , hence the function's name. To save the results next to your data, add output="predicted.csv" . If the file does have the class column, the result also includes the accuracy. That's all it takes: a file, a trained model, and the predicted classes.
docs.title: Step 2: Classify Samples Using the Trained Model

docs.text: Red Cedar can show which of your input features the model relies on to make its decisions: explanation = client.explainable.run(model["train_id"], verbose=True) for q in explanation["qubit_map"]: print(f"{q['feature_name']}: {q['importance']:.1%}") Each data qubit of the model encodes one input feature, and importance measures how much that qubit influences the prediction. By default Red Cedar first combines your columns into new features (principal components); train with settings={"dimension_reduction": "none"} to keep your own columns, so that the results name them. See Explainable AI in the User Guide.

docs.text: There is much more you can control. The User Guide covers it all; some places to start: Regression : predict a number instead of a class, with task="regression" . Settings : every training option (qubits, layers, the circuit structure, data preparation, training, execution) and how to set it. Evaluate a model : the accuracy per class, for any layer, or on a different backend. Analyze a dataset before training: how many dimensions carry signal, and how many qubits the model needs. Run on quantum hardware : train on a simulator, run on a quantum computer. The command line : redcedar train my_data.csv , without writing any Python. The Examples have notebooks for analyzing a dataset, the training settings, and training and evaluating a model in depth. © 2026 Cascade Quantum. All Rights Reserved.

docs.text: Release Notes Red Cedar is continually evolving, with issues fixed and enhancements made to add features. This section presents a brief record of relevant changes made to each version that has been released. Latest version is at the top. Version 0.9 Release Notes Version 0.9 is the first tagged version of Red Cedar. Each release below lists the changes since the one before it. Release 0.93 - in preparation Predictions on new data -- client.inference.run(train_id, "new_data.csv") returns a prediction for each row: the class label and the probability of each class, or a number for a regression model. When the file also has the target column, the result includes the accuracy (classification) or the mean absolute error (regression). Columns are matched by header name, or by position in a file without a header row. output="predictions.csv" writes the rows with their predictions. Evaluation renamed -- Scoring a model on the test rows held back from its training run is now client.training.evaluate(train_id) , and client.inference.run() makes predictions on new data. Code that called inference.run(train_id) for the test accuracy must change to training.evaluate(train_id) . The example notebooks are updated. Regression -- training.run(..., task="regression") trains a regression model. Without task= , the task is detected from the target column; whole numbers are read as classes, so pass task="regression" for a target of whole numbers. Evaluation, predictions and the training replay support regression models (loss and mean absolute error); explainable AI supports classification models only. Settings: num_qubits_target (default 2) and loss_type (default weighted_hamming ). Regression predictions are not useful yet in this release: on the Energy Efficiency example the model predicts about the same value for every sample, and its error is larger than that of predicting the average (see Known Issues ). Train on all rows -- test_size=0 trains the model on every row. The model then has no test set: the layer results have no test values, and training.evaluate() and training.analyze() report that there are no test rows. CSV files directly -- training.run() and inference.run() take a CSV file path and upload it. Command line -- The redcedar command: redcedar train , evaluate , predict and models (also python -m redcedar ). Connecting -- connect() defaults to http://127.0.0.1:8002 . A hosted server requires an API key (see Connecting to a Server ). connect(local=True) calls the Red Cedar code directly in your Python process, with no server, for development with the Red Cedar source ( pip install -e . in the red-cedar folder); see Local Mode . Quieter progress -- verbose=True now prints the progress line, a dot every few seconds while the job is working, and the test result after each training layer. The server's full log for the job, which verbose=True used to print, now needs verbose="log" ( --log on the command line). Explainable AI names principal components -- With dimension reduction ( dimension_reduction: "pca" , the default), a data qubit holds a principal component, a mix of all the dataset's columns. Explainable AI now names it PC1 , PC2 , ... and lists in made_of the columns with the largest shares of it, largest first; the web UI shows them in a table under the qubit mapping. With dimension_reduction: "none" , each data qubit holds one column and is named after it (see Explainable AI ). Examples -- The example notebooks are reworked and saved with the output of a run, so they can be read on GitHub. The Quick Start trains on classified samples, classifies the samples in a second file, and checks the predicted classes against their actual classes; quick_start.py does the same from the command line. 05_regression.ipynb shows the same steps for regression. The other notebooks follow the same structure, and 01_full_pipeline.ipynb is removed (see Examples ). Documentation -- The Quick Start's second step is "Classify Samples Using the Trained Model". The User Guide explains the training loss and accuracy, and what explainable AI's feature names mean with and without dimension reduction. Versions -- client.status() and redcedar status show the server's version and the SDK's. The SDK now follows the server's version number: this release is SDK 0.93.0 (it was 0.1.0), and SDK-only fixes get a new patch number (0.93.1, 0.93.2, ...). Bug fix: CUDA-Q server crash -- A server running on CUDA-Q could crash after several training jobs. Fixed. Bug fix: seeded CUDA-Q runs -- Two CUDA-Q runs with the same seed could give different results. Seeded runs now repeat. CUDA-Q explainable AI -- Explainable AI on CUDA-Q is seeded and uses 10000 shots, so repeated runs on the same model give the same result. The shot count is temporary and will become a setting. Bug fix: fractional targets in CSV files with a header row -- The target column of such a file was read as text, so a fractional regression target was detected as class labels. Targets that are numbers are now read as numbers. Bug fix: CSV files without a header row and with text class labels -- The class label in the last column (for example M ) made the first row look like a header, so the first sample was used as column names and not loaded. The header check now looks at the feature columns, and counts a text value at the top of the target column only when it doesn't occur again in that column (a column name, not a class label). Bug fix: split sizes for uploaded files -- train_size and test_size were ignored for uploaded CSV files, which always used the 80/20 split. Bug fix: explainable AI feature names -- With dimension reduction (the default), the numbers of the selected components were looked up in the dataset's column names, so a data qubit was labelled with a column it did not stand for (for example mean_radius for principal component 1). Components are now named as above. Bug fix: explainable AI importance for features with more than one qubit -- The importance values were shifted by one qubit for each extra qubit of a feature, and the last data qubit always showed 0%. Each qubit now gets its own value. Bug fix: web UI Job Management times and job types -- Times are shown in your local time zone (they were UTC without saying so), and each job is labelled with its type (training, inference, explainable AI, training analysis, PCA, mutual information, resource estimation). Release 0.92 - 2 November 2026 CUDA-Q results corrected -- On the CUDA-Q backend, the predicted class was read from the wrong qubit: a data qubit instead of the prediction qubit. Training on CUDA-Q was therefore scored against the wrong bit. Results are now read by qubit index, the same way as on Qiskit. On a 6-qubit WDBC test, CUDA-Q test accuracy went from 0.535 to 0.781 (Qiskit: 0.746). Models trained on CUDA-Q with an earlier version should be retrained. Models trained on Qiskit are not affected. Same bit order on Qiskit and CUDA-Q -- CUDA-Q circuits are now built so that their results come back in the same bit order as Qiskit, and results are no longer reversed after execution. Qiskit and CUDA-Q now give the same results for the same circuit, within shot noise. Seed and operator direction -- Two new training settings: seed , which sets the initial parameters, and op_direction ( backward , the default, or forward ). Both are saved with the model. With a seed set, repeated runs give the same result on Qiskit and on CUDA-Q. On CUDA-Q, the first seeded run after the server starts can differ slightly from later runs with the same seed. Shared optimizer for classification and regression -- Classification and regression now use the same optimizer and loss function code. Classification results are unchanged. The regression loss options are hamming , weighted_hamming and huber . Bug fix: regression workflow -- The command-line regression workflow ( workflow_regression/ ) failed with a TypeError at the final test step, after training had finished, so no results were saved. It now reports the test loss and saves results. Bug fix: queued jobs -- A queued job started only when another request reached the server, so with only Python client SDK jobs, a queued job could wait indefinitely. The next queued job now starts as soon as the running job finishes. Bug fix: job progress streams -- Progress events that arrived while the server was sending earlier events were dropped. Training curves could miss points, and a lost completion event left the client waiting. All events are now delivered, for both training and analysis jobs. Bug fix: CSV files without a header row -- Class labels from a CSV file with no header row were read as numbers, and saving the per-class results failed. Class labels are now strings for both kinds of file. Regression targets are unchanged. Circuits that contain a mid-circuit measurement now raise a clear error instead of returning shifted bits on hardware. Red Cedar circuits do not contain any today. New checks in tests/ for CUDA-Q bit order and class reading ( test_cudaq_bit_order.py , check_cudaq_class_read.py ), CUDA-Q results against an exact statevector ( test_cudaq_cct_exact.py ), Qiskit and CUDA-Q equivalence ( test_api_equivalence.py ), and explainable AI from start to finish on both APIs ( check_eai.py ). Release 0.91 - 28 September 2026 IQM hardware support -- Training and inference can run on IQM quantum computers (Garnet, Sirius, Emerald) through qiskit-iqm , using backend IDs such as iqm-garnet . Circuits are sent in batches of 100. The access token is read from IQM_API_TOKEN . Requires an additional package : pip install qiskit-iqm . Stop a running job -- A new endpoint, POST /jobs/{job_id}/stop , stops any running or queued job: training, inference or explainable AI. Data loading and preprocessing (preview) -- A new module, quantum_learning/data_loading/ , adds ClassicalData.load_data() , train/test splitting, preprocessing (including PCA that chooses the number of components automatically), bit-bit encoding transforms, settings with type checking, and saving and loading of preprocessing objects. The notebook advanced_data_loading.ipynb in the same folder shows how to use it. The training workflows and the server do not use it yet. Fixed server startup on Windows: run_server.bat now starts the server with python -m uvicorn . Release 0.90 - 23 September 2026 Version 0.9 is the base version from which versioning began. It provides a server for dataset analysis, training, inference and explainable AI, along with command-line workflows for classification and regression and a Python client SDK for notebooks and scripts. Models are defined as hierarchical operators rather than circuits and are synthesized for the selected backend; training uses sub-net initialization, bit-bit encoding of classical data, and exact coordinate update, with no classical optimizer. Circuits run on Qiskit simulators, on CUDA-Q (including multi-GPU execution), and on IonQ simulators and hardware. © 2026 Cascade Quantum. All Rights Reserved.

docs.text: User Guide This guide is the complete reference for the redcedar Python SDK: every call, its arguments and what it returns, the settings, and the command line. For a first walkthrough, start with the Quick Start . How Red Cedar Works A Red Cedar model is a parameterized quantum circuit that learns to map your input features to an answer. The SDK sends your data and settings to a Red Cedar server; the server prepares the data, builds the circuits, runs them on a simulator or a quantum computer, and trains the parameters. Results come back to the SDK as plain Python values (dicts and lists). The work has three steps, and the SDK groups its calls the same way: Step Call What it does Train training.run() Trains a model on your data. Evaluate (optional) training.evaluate() Scores the model on the rows held back from its own training run: how good is it? Use inference.run() Makes predictions on new rows you supply. training holds everything about building a model and judging it; inference holds using it. Alongside these are datasets , analysis (understanding a dataset before training) and explainable (what the model relies on). Long-running calls wait until the server has finished and then return the result. The server runs one job at a time; if it is busy, your job waits in a queue and starts when the job before it finishes. Installation pip install redcedar The only dependency is requests . The example notebooks also plot with matplotlib: pip install "redcedar[plotting]" . To read the source, or to work on the SDK itself, install it from a clone of the repository instead: git clone https://github.com/coherent-computing/redcedar.git cd redcedar pip install -e . Connecting to a Server A Server on Your Own Machine If you have the Red Cedar engine installed, start its server from the red-cedar folder with ./run_server.sh (Linux, Mac) or run_server.bat (Windows). It listens on port 8002, and the SDK connects to http://127.0.0.1:8002 by default. The server only accepts requests with the key that the script sets (the line export BACKEND_API_KEY=... in run_server.sh , set BACKEND_API_KEY=... in run_server.bat ). Pass the same key to connect() , or set it once as REDCEDAR_API_KEY : import redcedar client = redcedar.connect(api_key="<the BACKEND_API_KEY value from run_server.sh>") print(client.status()) # {'ok': True, 'server_version': '0.93', 'sdk_version': '0.93.0'} Without the key, status() and datasets.list() still work, but training, analysis, inference and explainable AI are refused ( 422 , no key; 403 , a wrong key). This key belongs to the server itself. A hosted server uses your personal API key instead (next section). status() also tells you which versions you are using: the server's version ( client.server_version gives it on its own) and the SDK's. The SDK's version follows the server's (SDK 0.93.x goes with server 0.93). In REDCEDAR_URL , use 127.0.0.1 rather than localhost for a server on your own machine. On Windows, localhost is tried first as IPv6 ( ::1 ), which the server doesn't listen on, and every request then waits about 2 seconds. A Hosted Server Pass the URL of the hosted server and your API key: client = redcedar.connect(url="https://<hosted-server-url>", api_key="your-api-key") Or set environment variables once, and call redcedar.connect() with no arguments: export REDCEDAR_URL="https://<hosted-server-url>" export REDCEDAR_API_KEY="your-api-key" Explicit arguments take priority over environment variables. A hosted server only accepts requests with a valid API key; without one, every call fails with 401 (no key or an unknown key) or 403 (a key without access). Getting a key. Contact your Cascade Quantum representative to get an API key, or to get access to the Red Cedar user interface. If you already have access to the user interface, you can create your own key there, under API Keys . Keep the key private: it acts as you. You have one key at a time; a new key replaces the old one, which then stops working. Local Mode, for Development With the Red Cedar source and its dependencies in your Python environment, the SDK can call the Red Cedar code directly, with no server. Install the source once, from the red-cedar folder: pip install -e . Then connect in local mode: client = redcedar.connect(local=True) Every SDK call then runs the same function the server runs for it, in your own Python process and thread: no server, no port, no HTTP. Results are the same as through a server, and a debugger steps from the SDK call straight into the Red Cedar code. Without the install, pass the folder instead ( connect(local="path/to/red-cedar") , or set REDCEDAR_CORE_PATH ). Local mode uses the datasets, trained models and job records of that red-cedar folder, the same ones a server started from it uses: a model trained through the server can be evaluated locally, and the other way round. Ctrl+C stops a local training run, as training.stop() does; the layers that finished are kept. Data Your Own Data Red Cedar trains on tables: one row per example, input features first, and the last column is the target , the answer the model learns. A CSV file is the usual way to provide one. Header row: optional. A first row counts as a header when any of its cells is text. With a header, Red Cedar knows your columns by name, which inference.run() uses to match new files and explainable AI uses to name features. Without one, columns are known by position only. One caveat: a file without a header whose last column holds text labels (such as M / B ) has text in its first row and would be read as having a header. Give such files a header row. Features are numbers. Red Cedar scales, normalizes and compresses them as part of training (see Data preparation under Settings). Pass the path of a CSV file wherever a dataset is expected: model = client.training.run("my_data.csv") The file is uploaded each time. To upload once and reuse it, use datasets.upload() , which returns a dataset ID: dataset_id = client.datasets.upload("my_data.csv") model = client.training.run(dataset_id, settings={"num_qubits": 6}) The Dataset Catalog The server also has a catalog of ready-to-use datasets, such as "wdbc" , "iris" and "diabetes" . for ds in client.datasets.list(): print(ds["id"], ds["name"], ds.get("rows"), ds.get("classes")) Each entry is a dict. The most useful fields: id , name , description , category , source , rows , columns , classes , available . The id is what you pass to the analysis and training calls. Training client.training.run(data, settings=None, verbose=False, on_progress=None, train_size=None, test_size=None, class_range=None, task=None) Trains a model and waits until training ends. Argument Type Default Description data str required A CSV file path, a dataset ID from datasets.upload() , or a catalog ID settings dict or str None Settings to change, as a dict or a .json / .toml file path (see Settings ) verbose bool or "log" False Print progress to stdout; "log" adds the server's log ( Progress ) on_progress callable None Called with (percent, message) on each update train_size float or int 0.8 Training set size, as a fraction or a number of rows test_size float or int 0.2 Test set size, as a fraction or a number of rows; 0 trains on all rows class_range list all classes Classes to train on, e.g. ["0", "1"] (catalog datasets only) task str detected "classification" or "regression" (see Classification or Regression ) model = client.training.run("my_data.csv", verbose=True, settings={ "num_qubits": 6, "min_layers": 1, "max_layers": 2, }) train_id = model["train_id"] Returns a dict with train_id , task , train_samples , test_samples , total_layers , elapsed_seconds , data_loading_seconds , plus: history : the training curves, by layer. Each layer has a list of {iteration, train_loss, train_accuracy} (no train_accuracy for regression). validation : the test results at the end of each layer, by layer: test_loss , test_accuracy , test_accuracy_per_class , test_loss_per_class , num_parameters and timings. Regression has test_loss only. With test_size=0 the test values are None . import matplotlib.pyplot as plt for layer, points in model["history"].items(): plt.plot([p["train_loss"] for p in points], label=f"layer {layer}") plt.xlabel("Iteration"); plt.ylabel("Training loss"); plt.legend() for layer, v in model["validation"].items(): print(f"Layer {layer}: test accuracy {v['test_accuracy']:.1%}") Training Loss and Accuracy While a model trains, Red Cedar measures two numbers on the training rows after every parameter update, and returns them in history : Training loss. For each row, the circuit gives a probability for every class. The row's loss is 1 minus the probability of its correct class: 0 when the model is certain of the right class, 1 when it gives that class no chance. The training loss is the average of these over the training rows, plus 10 times their variance. The variance term makes the optimizer prefer a model that does about equally well on every row over one that is very sure of some rows and wrong on others. Each parameter update is chosen to lower this loss. Training accuracy. The share of training rows whose correct class gets the highest probability, that is, the rows the model classifies correctly. The test loss and test accuracy in validation , and from training.evaluate() , are the same two measures on the rows held back from training. The training numbers are measured on rows the model learns from, so they usually look better than the test numbers; the test numbers tell you how the model will do on new data. On a plot of the training curves, the loss usually falls quickly at first and then levels off. Once a layer's curve is flat, more parameter updates in that layer change little. For a regression model, the loss measures how far the predicted number is from the target, as set by loss_type (default "weighted_hamming" ), and there is no training accuracy. Train and Test Rows Every training run splits the data: by default 80% of the rows train the model and 20% are held back for testing. The split is stratified by class (each class keeps its share in both parts) and is the same every time for the same data. The held-out rows are what training tests at the end of each layer, and what training.evaluate() scores. Holding rows back is what makes the test accuracy honest: accuracy measured on the training rows overstates how the model does on new data. The usual pattern when you want the final model to learn from everything: Train with the default split and check the test results. If they're good, train again with the same settings and test_size=0 , and use that model for predictions. With test_size=0 there is no held-out score: the test values in the layer results are None , and training.evaluate() and training.analyze() stop with an error saying the model has no test rows. To measure such a model, make predictions on rows that include the target column. Layers A model is trained one layer at a time, from min_layers to max_layers . Each layer adds a set of parameters to the circuit; by default ( chain_layers=True ) a layer starts from the parameters the layer before it found. Every finished layer is saved, and later calls take layer= to pick one (the highest by default). Classification or Regression The task is decided when the model is trained, and saved with it. Without task= , Red Cedar detects it from a CSV file's target column: text labels or whole numbers mean classification , numbers with fractions mean regression (catalog datasets are classification). A target of whole numbers that is really a quantity (a count, a score, a price in whole units) needs task="regression" : model = client.training.run("prices.csv", task="regression", settings={"num_qubits": 6}) task="classification" on a target with fractional numbers stops with an error, as does task="regression" on text labels. A regression model predicts a number. The circuit encodes the target as a binary number on num_qubits_target qubits (default 2, taken from num_qubits ); the prediction is the average of that number over the measured outcomes, scaled to the range of the training targets, so predictions stay between the smallest and largest target seen in training. Its test result is a loss ( loss_type , default "weighted_hamming" ); training.evaluate() and inference.run() also give the mean absolute error, in the target's units. Explainable AI works with classification models only. client.training.status(train_id) and client.training.stop(train_id) status() returns train_id , status ( running , completed , failed or stopped ), progress , summary and error_message . A job still waiting in the queue has no status yet (404). stop() asks the server to stop a running training job; finished layers are kept. Since training.run() waits until the job ends, call stop() from another thread, notebook or process. The waiting training.run() then raises RuntimeError("Training stopped") . Evaluating a Model Training already reports the test accuracy after each layer. The calls in this section look at a trained model again, later, in more detail. client.training.evaluate(train_id, layer=None, settings=None, verbose=False, on_progress=None) Scores a trained model on the rows held back from its training run. You pass no data: the server rebuilds the same split from the model's saved settings. Argument Type Default Description train_id str required The model, from training.run() layer int highest layer Which layer of the model to score settings dict None Execution settings only ( backend , parallelize ), e.g. to score on a different backend verbose bool or "log" False Print progress to stdout; "log" adds the server's log ( Progress ) on_progress callable None Called with (percent, message) on each update report = client.training.evaluate(train_id, verbose=True) print(report["overall_accuracy"]) print(report["test_samples"]) for cls in report["per_class"]: print(f"Class {cls['class']}: {cls['accuracy']:.1%} ({cls['samples']} samples)") Returns a dict with train_id , layer , task , overall_accuracy , overall_loss , test_samples , num_classes , per_class (a list of dicts with class , accuracy , loss , samples ), and timings. For a regression model, overall_accuracy is None , per_class is empty, and mean_absolute_error gives the average error in the target's units. It reports on the held-out rows as a whole; for a result per row, use inference.run() . At most 400 held-out rows are scored. client.training.analyze(train_id, layer=None, verbose=False, on_progress=None) Replays the parameters saved during training on the held-out rows, giving the test accuracy and loss over the course of training. layer defaults to the highest layer. replay = client.training.analyze(train_id) plt.plot(replay["accuracy_history"]) plt.xlabel("Checkpoint"); plt.ylabel("Test accuracy") Returns a dict with train_id , layer , num_checkpoints , accuracy_history , loss_history , final_accuracy , final_loss , and timings. Regression models have a loss history only. Predictions client.inference.run(train_id, data, layer=None, output=None, settings=None, verbose=False, on_progress=None) Runs a trained model on new rows and returns one result per row. Argument Type Default Description train_id str required The model, from training.run() data str required A CSV file path, or a dataset ID from datasets.upload() layer int highest layer Which layer of the model to use output str None Also write the results to this CSV file settings dict None Execution settings only ( backend , parallelize ) verbose bool or "log" False Print progress to stdout; "log" adds the server's log ( Progress ) on_progress callable None Called with (percent, message) on each update predictions = client.inference.run(train_id, "new_data.csv", output="predictions.csv") for row in predictions["predictions"][:5]: print(row["prediction"], row["probabilities"]) Returns a dict with train_id , layer , task , rows , timings, and predictions , a list with one entry per row, in the order of the file: Classification: {"prediction": "M", "probabilities": {"M": 0.81, "B": 0.19}} . The labels are the ones in the training data. Regression: {"prediction": 152.3} . If the new rows also contain the target column, the result has an accuracy as well (regression: a mean_absolute_error ). The output file holds the input columns plus a prediction column and, for classification, one probability_<class> column per class. The new rows are prepared exactly as the training data was (scaling, compression, encoding), using the training data, which must therefore still be on the server. Matching the Columns of a New File The model has to pair each column of the new file with one of its inputs: The file has a header row (a first row that is all text): columns are matched by name. They can be in any order. Columns the model doesn't use (an ID, say) are ignored. A missing feature column stops with an error naming it. If the target column is present (under its training name), the accuracy is reported too. No header row: columns are matched by position. The columns must be the training features in training order, optionally followed by the target column. Any other number of columns stops with an error saying how many were expected. A model trained on a file without a header knows its columns by position only, so its new files are matched by position too. client.inference.models() Lists the six most recently trained models on the server. for m in client.inference.models()["models"]: print(m["train_id"], m.get("dataset_display_name"), m.get("num_qubits"), m.get("layers")) Each entry includes train_id , dataset , dataset_display_name , num_qubits , layers (the completed layer numbers), max_layer , node_order , timestamp , non_defaults (the settings that differ from the defaults) and training_params . Trained models are not kept forever: see Known Issues for how long a server keeps them. Explainable AI client.explainable.run(train_id, settings=None, verbose=False, on_progress=None) Shows which input features drive the model's decisions. It uses the highest layer of the model. Each data qubit is mapped back to the input feature it encodes, and importance measures how much that qubit influences the prediction. What a data qubit encodes depends on the dimension_reduction setting. With "dimension_reduction": "none" , each data qubit encodes one of your columns, and feature_name is that column's name. By default ( "pca" ), the columns are first combined into principal components, each a mix of all of them: feature_name is the component ( PC1 , PC2 , ...), and made_of lists the columns with the largest shares of it, largest first, with the rest summed: {"parts": [{"feature": "worst_perimeter", "share": 0.49}, {"feature": "worst_radius", "share": 0.23}, ...], "others": {"count": 26, "share": 0.13}} The shares of all the columns add up to 1. A component with one or two large shares stands mostly for those columns; one with many small shares is a broad mix. Argument Type Default Description train_id str required The model, from training.run() settings dict None Execution settings only ( backend , parallelize ) verbose bool or "log" False Print progress to stdout; "log" adds the server's log ( Progress ) on_progress callable None Called with (percent, message) on each update explanation = client.explainable.run(train_id, verbose=True) for q in explanation["qubit_map"]: print(f"Qubit {q['qubit']}: {q['feature_name']} (importance {q['importance']:.1%})") for qid, val in explanation["convergence"].items(): print(f"Class qubit {qid}: convergence = {val:.4f}") Returns a dict with train_id , layer , dataset_name , num_qubits , num_class_qubits , class_range , qubit_map (a list of dicts with qubit , feature_index , feature_name , bits , bit , made_of , importance ), convergence (class qubit ID to convergence value), distributions , feature_indices , and timings. Dataset Analysis Three calls help you understand a dataset before training. All three take a catalog ID or a dataset ID from datasets.upload() , plus verbose and on_progress . client.analysis.pca(dataset_id) Principal Component Analysis: how many independent dimensions carry real signal in the data. pca = client.analysis.pca("wdbc", verbose=True) print(pca["features"]) # 30 print(pca["thresholds"]["90"]) # 7 (components for 90% of the variance) Returns dataset_name , features , samples , n_components , variance_ratios , cumulative_variance , thresholds (percentage to number of components), and timings. client.analysis.mi(dataset_id) Mutual information. The data is first reduced with PCA, as training does, and each principal component ( PC1 , PC2 , ...) is ranked by how strongly it predicts the target. mi = client.analysis.mi("wdbc", verbose=True) for f in mi["ranked_features"][:5]: print(f["feature_name"], f["mi_score"]) Returns dataset_name , samples , features , classes , total_mi , ranked_features (with rank , feature_index , feature_name , mi_score , mi_percent ), cumulative_mi , thresholds , and timings. client.analysis.qre(dataset_id) Quantum resource estimation: how many qubits the model needs for this dataset. The data is encoded with more and more qubits until no two rows with different classes look the same (so 100% accuracy is possible in principle), plus the qubits needed for the class. The result is averaged over 10 random train/test splits. qre = client.analysis.qre("wdbc", verbose=True) print(qre["estimatedQubits"], "+/-", qre["standardDeviation"]) Returns dataset_name , estimatedQubits , standardDeviation , samples , features , classes , plotData (the highest possible train and test accuracy for each number of data qubits), warning_message , and timings. Settings The calls above work with no settings at all. Every part of a model can also be set: the circuit and its architecture, how the data is prepared, how training runs, and where the circuits execute. Passing Settings Settings are a Python dict, or the path of a .json or .toml file. Only the keys you give change; everything else keeps its default. Keys the server doesn't recognize are ignored without an error, so check the spelling against the tables below. # Dict client.training.run("my_data.csv", settings={"num_qubits": 8, "seed": 123}) # JSON file client.training.run("my_data.csv", settings="my_settings.json") # TOML file (Python 3.11+, or the tomli package) client.training.run("my_data.csv", settings="my_settings.toml") Every trained model saves its full settings, so any run can be repeated, or used as the starting point for the next one. training.run() takes all settings. training.evaluate() , inference.run() and explainable.run() use the model's own settings, fixed when it was trained; their settings= changes only how the circuits are run ( backend , parallelize ). Circuit and Architecture Key Default Description num_qubits 4 Number of qubits in the circuit min_layers 1 First layer in the layer sweep max_layers 2 Last layer in the layer sweep chain_layers True Start each layer from the parameters the layer before it found ( False : each layer starts from scratch) circuit_structure "bipartite" How the circuit's nodes are arranged ansatz_type "euler_and_heisenberg" Gate ansatz of the parameterized circuit activation_type "discretize" Activation function node_order_type "sequential" Order in which the optimizer visits the nodes op_direction "backward" Order of the ansatz operators over the data qubits ( "backward" or "forward" ) Data Preparation Key Default Description normalize True Normalize features to the [0, 1] range scale True Scale features before dimension reduction copula True Apply a copula transform to the training data dimension_reduction "pca" Dimension reduction method ( "pca" or "none" ) num_pca auto Number of PCA components bits_type "importance" How features are mapped to qubits The split into training and test rows is set with the train_size , test_size and class_range arguments of training.run() . Training Key Default Description num_iterations all nodes Optimizer iterations per layer all_nodes False Optimize all nodes (ignores num_iterations ) batch_size None Training rows per batch ( None : all training rows) seed None Seed for the initial parameters, so runs can be repeated ( None : random start) Regression Key Default Description num_qubits_target 2 Qubits that encode the target, out of num_qubits loss_type "weighted_hamming" Regression loss: "weighted_hamming" , "hamming" or "huber" Execution Key Default Description backend "statevector" Where the circuits run (see below) parallelize False Run circuits in parallel Running on Quantum Hardware The backend setting chooses where circuits run. "statevector" , the default, is an exact simulator. Other backends include "ionq-simulator" , IonQ quantum computers, and IQM quantum computers ( "iqm-garnet" , "iqm-sirius" , "iqm-emerald" ). Which backends a server offers depends on how it is set up and which provider accounts it has. Hardware time is expensive, and training runs many circuits. A common pattern is to train on a simulator, then evaluate the trained model, or make predictions, on hardware: model = client.training.run("my_data.csv", settings={"num_qubits": 6}) report = client.training.evaluate(model["train_id"], settings={"backend": "iqm-garnet"}) print(report["overall_accuracy"]) On hardware, results are estimated from shots and carry noise, so they differ somewhat from the exact simulator. Command Line Installing the SDK also installs the redcedar command, for training and predictions without writing Python. It uses the same server connection ( REDCEDAR_URL , REDCEDAR_API_KEY ). redcedar train my_data.csv --qubits 6 --layers 2 --seed 123 redcedar evaluate <train_id> redcedar predict <train_id> new_data.csv -o predictions.csv redcedar models redcedar status Command Same as Flags redcedar train training.run() ; prints the test result per layer and the train_id --qubits , --layers N (layers 1 to N), --seed , --backend , --task , --test-size , --settings redcedar evaluate training.evaluate() --layer , --backend redcedar predict inference.run() ; prints the predictions, or writes them with -o --layer , --backend , -o redcedar models inference.models() redcedar status status() ; prints the server's URL and version and the SDK version Any setting can come from a file: --settings my_settings.toml . Before the command, --url and --api-key choose the server, --local uses local mode , -q turns off the progress output, and --log adds the server's log for the job. Run redcedar <command> --help for the details. If the redcedar command isn't found (pip's scripts folder isn't on your PATH, which is common on Windows and with conda), use python -m redcedar instead: python -m redcedar train my_data.csv . Progress and Errors Progress All long-running calls take verbose and on_progress , which can be used together: verbose=True prints a single updating line, such as [ 30%] Layer 1/2 , and the test result after each layer of a training run. While the job is working, a dot is added to the line every few seconds (every 2 seconds at first, then every 5, then every 10 on a long step). While the job waits in the queue it prints Waiting in queue... . verbose="log" prints the same, plus the server's full log for the job (the training output of every iteration, timings, the model's structure). It's meant for finding out what went wrong. on_progress is called with (percent, message) on each update, for your own progress bars or logging. def my_callback(percent, message): log.info(f"{percent}% - {message}") model = client.training.run("my_data.csv", verbose=True, on_progress=my_callback) Errors The SDK raises standard Python exceptions: requests.ConnectionError : the server can't be reached. Use client.status() to check before starting work. requests.HTTPError : the server returned an error, such as 404 for a training job that doesn't exist or 401 for a wrong API key. RuntimeError : a job failed (the server's error message is included), or it was stopped with training.stop() ( "Training stopped" ). try: model = client.training.run("my_data.csv", verbose=True) except RuntimeError as e: print(f"Training failed: {e}") Limitations Some things are not possible yet: explainable AI for regression models, your own data loaders and custom circuit components (only CSV files and the catalog, and the built-in components chosen by settings), stopping jobs other than training, and keeping models on a server indefinitely. docs.text: A Red Cedar model is a parameterized quantum circuit that learns to map your input features to an answer. The SDK sends your data and settings to a Red Cedar server; the server prepares the data, builds the circuits, runs them on a simulator or a quantum computer, and trains the parameters. Results come back to the SDK as plain Python values (dicts and lists). The work has three steps, and the SDK groups its calls the same way: Step Call What it does Train training.run() Trains a model on your data. Evaluate (optional) training.evaluate() Scores the model on the rows held back from its own training run: how good is it? Use inference.run() Makes predictions on new rows you supply. training holds everything about building a model and judging it; inference holds using it. Alongside these are datasets , analysis (understanding a dataset before training) and explainable (what the model relies on). Long-running calls wait until the server has finished and then return the result. The server runs one job at a time; if it is busy, your job waits in a queue and starts when the job before it finishes.
docs.title: How Red Cedar Works

docs.text: pip install redcedar The only dependency is requests . The example notebooks also plot with matplotlib: pip install "redcedar[plotting]" . To read the source, or to work on the SDK itself, install it from a clone of the repository instead: git clone https://github.com/coherent-computing/redcedar.git cd redcedar pip install -e .
docs.title: Installation

docs.text: If you have the Red Cedar engine installed, start its server from the red-cedar folder with ./run_server.sh (Linux, Mac) or run_server.bat (Windows). It listens on port 8002, and the SDK connects to http://127.0.0.1:8002 by default. The server only accepts requests with the key that the script sets (the line export BACKEND_API_KEY=... in run_server.sh , set BACKEND_API_KEY=... in run_server.bat ). Pass the same key to connect() , or set it once as REDCEDAR_API_KEY : import redcedar client = redcedar.connect(api_key="<the BACKEND_API_KEY value from run_server.sh>") print(client.status()) # {'ok': True, 'server_version': '0.93', 'sdk_version': '0.93.0'} Without the key, status() and datasets.list() still work, but training, analysis, inference and explainable AI are refused ( 422 , no key; 403 , a wrong key). This key belongs to the server itself. A hosted server uses your personal API key instead (next section). status() also tells you which versions you are using: the server's version ( client.server_version gives it on its own) and the SDK's. The SDK's version follows the server's (SDK 0.93.x goes with server 0.93). In REDCEDAR_URL , use 127.0.0.1 rather than localhost for a server on your own machine. On Windows, localhost is tried first as IPv6 ( ::1 ), which the server doesn't listen on, and every request then waits about 2 seconds.
docs.title: A Server on Your Own Machine

docs.text: Pass the URL of the hosted server and your API key: client = redcedar.connect(url="https://<hosted-server-url>", api_key="your-api-key") Or set environment variables once, and call redcedar.connect() with no arguments: export REDCEDAR_URL="https://<hosted-server-url>" export REDCEDAR_API_KEY="your-api-key" Explicit arguments take priority over environment variables. A hosted server only accepts requests with a valid API key; without one, every call fails with 401 (no key or an unknown key) or 403 (a key without access). Getting a key. Contact your Cascade Quantum representative to get an API key, or to get access to the Red Cedar user interface. If you already have access to the user interface, you can create your own key there, under API Keys . Keep the key private: it acts as you. You have one key at a time; a new key replaces the old one, which then stops working.
docs.title: A Hosted Server

docs.text: With the Red Cedar source and its dependencies in your Python environment, the SDK can call the Red Cedar code directly, with no server. Install the source once, from the red-cedar folder: pip install -e . Then connect in local mode: client = redcedar.connect(local=True) Every SDK call then runs the same function the server runs for it, in your own Python process and thread: no server, no port, no HTTP. Results are the same as through a server, and a debugger steps from the SDK call straight into the Red Cedar code. Without the install, pass the folder instead ( connect(local="path/to/red-cedar") , or set REDCEDAR_CORE_PATH ). Local mode uses the datasets, trained models and job records of that red-cedar folder, the same ones a server started from it uses: a model trained through the server can be evaluated locally, and the other way round. Ctrl+C stops a local training run, as training.stop() does; the layers that finished are kept.
docs.title: Local Mode, for Development

docs.text: Red Cedar trains on tables: one row per example, input features first, and the last column is the target , the answer the model learns. A CSV file is the usual way to provide one. Header row: optional. A first row counts as a header when any of its cells is text. With a header, Red Cedar knows your columns by name, which inference.run() uses to match new files and explainable AI uses to name features. Without one, columns are known by position only. One caveat: a file without a header whose last column holds text labels (such as M / B ) has text in its first row and would be read as having a header. Give such files a header row. Features are numbers. Red Cedar scales, normalizes and compresses them as part of training (see Data preparation under Settings). Pass the path of a CSV file wherever a dataset is expected: model = client.training.run("my_data.csv") The file is uploaded each time. To upload once and reuse it, use datasets.upload() , which returns a dataset ID: dataset_id = client.datasets.upload("my_data.csv") model = client.training.run(dataset_id, settings={"num_qubits": 6})

docs.text: The server also has a catalog of ready-to-use datasets, such as "wdbc" , "iris" and "diabetes" . for ds in client.datasets.list(): print(ds["id"], ds["name"], ds.get("rows"), ds.get("classes")) Each entry is a dict. The most useful fields: id , name , description , category , source , rows , columns , classes , available . The id is what you pass to the analysis and training calls.
